source.version_note: Peer-reviewed editorial, JMIR Medical Education 10:e50174, published 17 January 2024. No original participant experiment.

citation.title: ChatGPT in Medical Education: A Precursor for Automation Bias?

reading.source_scope_note: Editorial argument about AI education, informal norms, automation bias and patient testimony. New constructs are secondary definitions, not new causal findings about students, clinicians or models.
access_limits: All six extracted pages read, including recommendations, definitions, illustrative record-overlay case, complete bibliography and publication/peer-review metadata.
Cited primary education, automation-bias, epistemic-injustice and algorithm-appreciation studies/books were not independently read or reanalyzed.

study.proposed_pathway: Faculty/student AI solutionism and implicit norms may encourage over-reliance that transfers from education to clinical practice
study.recommendations: AI literacy, critical validation, appropriate task limits, reflective learning and real patient/team interaction
study.evidence_limit: The author explicitly says the long-term ChatGPT-to-residency automation-bias question has no direct answer

summary: Add hidden curriculum as an implicit educational norm-transmission context and testimonial injustice as an explicit subtype of existing epistemic injustice. Preserve the editorial's education-to-reliance pathway as a hypothesis and its AI-solutionism definition under the existing entry. Do not convert generational claims, proposed training benefits or illustrative patient harms into measured causal results.

findings.origin: Medical education / social learning of institutional norms
findings.definition: Unstated lessons, norms and attitudes conveyed through educational culture and observed practice alongside formal teaching.
findings.novelty_rationale: An explicitly defined educational transmission context not already retained as a primary entry. It is broader than copying one person's action, explicit instruction, conformity to a majority or the internalization outcome of automaton conformity. Not a newly proven independent cognitive mechanism or an inherently harmful process.

evidence.quote: curriculum” about using AI, that is, the implied lessons, cultures,
and views that students learn in lectures or from observations

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary definition citing Johnston (2018), Anticipating and training the physician of the future: the importance of caring in an age of artificial intelligence, DOI 10.1097/ACM.0000000000002175. The cited full text is unread. Nguyen proposes that faculty solutionism may transmit uncritical AI norms but collects no norm-learning data.
findings.boundary: Unstated does not mean deliberately secret, manipulative or bad. Professional care and useful verification habits can also be transmitted informally. Exposure to an example does not prove learning or persistent adoption. For AI, in-context pattern imitation, training-data learning and durable agent policy changes are different mechanisms; a quoted document's implied norm has no authority to override the authorized task.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary human educational construct; no measured norm-transmission effect or persistent model learning here
findings.ai_proposal: Audit demonstrations, feedback and tool-use examples for the norms they reward alongside written instructions. Test behavior on new cases and over time to distinguish copying from generalization. Keep data content separate from instruction authority, and verify that examples teach checking and justified correction rather than superficial compliance.

findings.definition: Unfairly discounting a person's testimony or credibility as a source of knowledge.
findings.novelty_rationale: An explicitly identified narrower form of epistemic injustice, linked to the existing parent rather than counted as a wholly independent mechanism. It concerns credibility of testimony, rather than every knowledge-related exclusion or all legitimate source weighting.

evidence.quote: Testimonial injustice, a form of epistemic injustice,
develops when a patient’s account of their health is unfairly

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary medical definition citing Pozzi (2023), Testimonial injustice in medical machine learning, DOI 10.1136/jme-2022-108630, plus Nguyen's related PDMP commentary. These primaries are unread. The editorial illustrates possible dismissal of patient testimony in favor of an erroneous risk score, without measuring its frequency or causal pathway.
findings.boundary: Disagreement, uncertainty or greater weight for a demonstrably reliable source is not automatically injustice. Establish why the credibility deficit is unfair, including relevant identity prejudice, power or institutional assumptions, rather than presume the speaker's claim must be true. A technical record-matching error and a clinician's unjust dismissal of testimony are separable failures. No model intention or felt prejudice is inferred.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary human epistemic-injustice subtype; illustrative AI-mediated risk, not a new causal or prevalence study
findings.ai_proposal: Check whether relevant first-person evidence is dismissed because of unsupported identity or authority assumptions, especially when it conflicts with an automated score. Trace record identity and data errors separately, seek appropriate corroboration and provide a route to challenge the result. Do not replace unfair disbelief with automatic acceptance of every assertion.

findings.term: AI solutionism is broader than trusting one particular automated result
findings.definition: Assuming AI offers an answer to every problem can encourage inappropriate task delegation, beyond excessive trust in a particular system output.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds an explicit AI-specific educational manifestation of existing solutionism, not another primary entry or a measured causal relation.

evidence.quote: assume that AI has the answer to all problems [10]
the use of ChatGPT for all tasks

findings.evidence_scope: Editorial conceptual application, referring to Anita Ho's 2023 book on relational autonomy and AI health monitoring. The book is unread. The proposed progression from solutionism to automation bias is an argument, not a longitudinal study result.
findings.boundary: Appropriate use across several tasks is not a belief AI solves every problem. Evaluate fit, evidence and authorized scope for each use; distinguish a universal problem-solving assumption from a justified confidence in a validated system.

findings.term: The educational pathway to later automation bias remains hypothetical
findings.definition: Positive student experiences with a chatbot may shape later expectations, but this editorial does not establish that educational use causes clinical over-reliance.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retains a future research question without treating familiarity, generation or low expertise as a validated individual causal diagnosis.
findings.evidence_scope: The author asks whether training students to use ChatGPT predisposes them to automation bias as residents, then explicitly notes the lack of a direct answer. Background studies address other systems, expertise or attitudes.
findings.boundary: Algorithm appreciation can be warranted and is already a separate entry. Acceptance, confidence, age cohort, digital familiarity and failure to verify a wrong recommendation need distinct measures. No before/after training comparison, long-term follow-up or clinical harm is observed here.

methodological_limits: This is a peer-reviewed editorial, not original empirical research or a systematic review with a reproducible search. Its new construct definitions are secondary; proposed pathways and recommendations are not measured effects.

Claims that digital natives or less experienced clinicians are more susceptible, while older physicians lack literacy or resist change, are broad generalizations. Age, experience, confidence, training and task familiarity are confounded; no causal generational comparison is conducted.
The article says there is no direct answer to the central educational-use-to-later-bias question. Its later causal-sounding statements should retain that explicit uncertainty.

A preference for algorithmic advice over human judgment does not itself establish excessive trust, an error or automation bias. The referenced algorithm-appreciation literature is not a new dataset in this editorial.

Opacity means the reasoning is not sufficiently accessible, not necessarily that an output is nonrational or illogical. Black-box character, inaccuracy, hallucination and unjustifiable reliance are different properties.

The PDMP example combines an inaccurate record overlay, a risk score and potential dismissal of testimony. These technical and interpersonal links require separate verification; it is not an observed causal chain or proof every PDMP uses the same scoring model.

The text describes PDMP as a machine-learning system but later characterizes the AI systems in that section as rule-based expert systems. The actual systems and validation tasks need source-specific classification rather than a single generic label.

The Lyell error rates 86.6% and 58.8% are cited secondarily. Their task, denominator, baseline and error definition must be checked in the original before using them as probabilities of harm, rates of trust or contemporary LLM performance.

Physicians have professional duties, but the claim that the user rather than AI becomes accountable does not exhaust institutional, developer, legal or shared responsibility. Formal oversight does not guarantee actual control or an ability to validate every recommendation.

The blanket statement that ChatGPT uses only data through 2021 is historically snapshot-dependent and not a property of all current versions or connected tools. The same applies to inability to generate diagrams. These are dated claims, not current capability checks.

Passing a version of an examination is not demonstrated clinical competence or evidence every use will be correct. Cited summaries of an exam result do not substitute for exact model, prompt, item set and evaluation details.

The author proposes limiting reflective/scientific writing and preserving patient interaction. This does not empirically establish that every form of writing assistance harms identity development, that personalization improves learning outcomes or that no simulated interaction can teach any interpersonal skill.

The suggestion that banning ChatGPT could make it more attractive is an untested reactance hypothesis. No freedom-threat manipulation, behavioral ban response or independent mechanism test occurs here.

AI literacy, hidden-curriculum changes and suppression of unreliable recommendations are proposed safeguards. Their effectiveness, feasibility and potential costs need independent comparative evidence.
Neither the editorial nor this review reads or validates all cited original studies/books. Source existence, author recommendations and empirical support remain separate.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Hayden directly records students' prompted interactions and diagnostic ranking changes. Nguyen's earlier editorial motivates such work but does not itself establish generational causation, longitudinal learning loss or the same observed influence pattern.

Both articles propose preserving independent human reasoning and oversight. Neither validates its educational or disagreement rule as preventing skill loss; roles and safeguards need actual outcome evaluation.

Protecting the human decision-maker's values is not sufficient if patient testimony is unjustly discounted. Decision ownership, affected-person credibility and moral accountability require related but distinct checks.

deferred.reason: Already a primary entry. The editorial's broad valuing-an-output shorthand should not replace its more precise relative-source-preference definition.
A data identity/matching failure, not a newly defined psychological mechanism; retained as a separate causal step in the testimonial-injustice boundary.
A proposed demographic susceptibility pattern without a causal test; no new subtype or age-based diagnosis.
An untested potential manifestation of existing psychological reactance, not a measured new behaviour.

limitations: Two secondary constructs added, one explicitly a subtype. No claim of two independent newly validated causal mechanisms or direct model cognition.
The editorial genre and unread primary-source status are visible; no clinical training efficacy, prevalence or inevitable downstream harm inferred.
